scenario.context: The player enters the Glasshouse Research Lab of the Arcanum Institute. Dr. Lira Voss, a senior chronomancer, is hunched over a massive, humming chronometer prototype that has been running erratically for weeks.
scenario.text: "We've poured three full grant cycles—over two hundred thousand crystal shards—into this chronometer," Dr. Voss says, gesturing at the tangled array of quartz lenses. "The Institute offered us a compact, field‑tested temporal stabilizer from the Meridian Guild for a fraction of the cost. But I've already invested so much time, reputation, and resources. If we abandon this now, all that work evaporates. Just a few more calibrations, maybe a new power core, and we'll finally get the phase lock right. I can't let those months go to waste," she adds, eyes fixed on the flickering display.
scenario.speaker_context: Dr. Lira Voss is a brilliant but prideful researcher whose identity is tightly bound to the success of her chronometer project.

structure.pattern_description: Dr. Voss treats the past investment of grant cycles, time, and reputation as a justification to keep funding a failing prototype, ignoring that those costs are sunk and that a proven alternative exists at much lower future cost.
structure.why_wrong: The resources already spent cannot be recovered regardless of the decision. Continuing to invest because of past expenditure can lead to greater losses than switching to the proven stabilizer, which offers better expected outcomes with lower future cost.
structure.counterpoint: If the prototype were only a minor tweak away from success and the additional cost were negligible, persisting could be rational. The fallacy appears when the decision is driven primarily by past investment rather than future benefit.

assessment.identification_prompt: Dr. Voss lists several reasons for continuing work on the chronometer. Identify which reasons are based on sunk costs and explain whether they actually indicate that continuing is a good choice.

rubric.description: Agrees with Dr. Voss, saying the past investment alone makes quitting impossible.
Notes that Dr. Voss is stubborn but cannot pinpoint the logical error.
Recognizes that the decision should be based on future costs/benefits, but does not label the bias.
Correctly identifies the sunk‑cost reasoning and explains why it is irrelevant to the decision.
Identifies the bias, articulates the formal fallacy, and proposes a forward‑looking decision framework.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: The lab assistant whispers, "Sometimes we cling to what we've built, but the crystals we spent are already gone. What matters now is which path gives us the most stable timeline for the least future cost."
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Dr. Voss sighs, "You're right. I’ve been letting the past dictate my choices. Perhaps we should test the Meridian stabilizer and allocate the remaining grant to other projects."

game_hooks.npc_personality: Intelligent, proud, emotionally attached to her work, slightly defensive when challenged.
npc_dialogue_seed: I can't just throw away three grant cycles.
If we switch now, all that effort will be for nothing.
Just a few more tweaks and it'll work.
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player can (a) allocate additional lab resources to keep the chronometer alive, (b) persuade Dr. Voss to purchase the Meridian stabilizer, or (c) propose a hybrid test that uses the stabilizer as a backup while finishing a limited set of calibrations.

scenario.context: The player arrives at the training grounds of the Golden Hawks, a semi‑professional football team. The team's trainer, Milo "Boost" Harrow, has just unveiled a new "miracle" protein shake that he claims will give players an extra burst of speed and stamina for the upcoming match.
scenario.text:
"Listen up, squad!" Milo shouts, holding up a bright‑blue bottle. "This is the Hawk's Edge shake—made from secret herbs and a dash of starlight. One sip before the game and you'll feel like you can outrun the wind!" He hands the bottle to the nervous midfielder, Jace, who gulps it down and immediately smiles. Later, during the scrimmage, Jace makes sharper passes and looks more confident, though his heart rate and sprint times are unchanged. After the drill, Milo pats Jace on the back. "See? I told you the shake works!" The veteran captain, Lena, watches skeptically and asks for a bottle. Milo sighs, "Sorry, I only have enough for the ones who truly believe it will help."
"But what if it's just water with a splash of fruit juice?" Lena whispers to the player.
"It doesn't matter," Milo replies, grinning. "The belief is the real power."
scenario.speaker_context: Milo is demonstrating the placebo effect: players improve mentally because they expect the shake to work, even though the drink has no performance‑enhancing ingredients. Their confidence rises, but objective physical metrics stay the same.

structure.pattern_description: The placebo effect occurs when a person experiences real improvement due to the expectation of benefit, not because of any active component in the treatment. It is "dual" because the belief can produce genuine psychological benefits while simultaneously masking the lack of physiological effect.
structure.formal_form: Athlete A consumes drink D (no active ingredients). A believes D enhances performance. Belief B increases confidence and focus, leading to observable behavioral improvements (e.g., better decision‑making). Physiological metrics (speed, endurance) remain unchanged, showing the limitation of the effect.
structure.why_wrong: Relying on the shake can create false confidence, hide underlying fitness deficits, and potentially lead to overexertion or injury when the expected physical boost never arrives.
structure.why_right: The confidence boost can reduce anxiety, improve focus, and foster a positive mindset, all of which are valuable for teamwork and decision‑making during a match.
structure.counterpoint: When might this heuristic be useful? It can be strategically employed to calm nerves before high‑pressure moments, such as penalty kicks, where mental composure can outweigh marginal physical gains.

assessment.identification_prompt: Which cognitive bias explains why the players feel better after drinking Milo's "miracle" shake even though the drink contains only water and fruit juice?

rubric.description: No identification or irrelevant answer.
Mentions that belief influences performance but does not name the bias.
Identifies the phenomenon as a "placebo" effect but provides an incomplete explanation.
Correctly names the Placebo effect and notes that belief, not ingredients, drives the observed change.
Accurately names the Placebo effect, explains both its beneficial mental impact and its limitation (no physiological enhancement), and links it to the players' behavior in the scenario.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Milo chuckles, "The shake is just flavored water, but look at Jace—he's playing with his head in the game now. Sometimes belief is the real power, even if the bottle is empty."
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Milo nods approvingly, "Exactly! The confidence you felt is real, even though the drink itself does nothing. That's the placebo effect in action—mind over matter, with limits."

game_hooks.npc_personality: Boisterous, hype‑driven, loves rallying the team with grand claims, but genuinely believes morale is the key to victory.
npc_dialogue_seed: "One sip and you'll feel the wind at your back!"
"If you don't believe it, it won't work—just like that!"
"The secret's not in the bottle, it's in your head!"
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player can (a) give the shake to a skeptical teammate who refuses, observing no change, or (b) compare sprint times and heart‑rate data before and after the shake to see that only confidence improves. Either path reveals the dual nature of the placebo effect.

scenario.context: During a sudden flood in the port city of Rivermist, the player meets Captain Mara, the fire brigade leader, who must decide how to allocate limited rescue boats to two districts.
scenario.text:
Captain Mara looks over a parchment. "If we send three boats to the market district, we can rescue 120 of the 150 people trapped there. That's a 80% success rate. I think we should prioritize that area," she says, her voice steady. A nearby clerk, Joren, interjects, "But if we keep those three boats here, 30 families in the lower docks will lose everything. That's 30 lives we can't bring back. We should send the boats to the docks instead."
The player can choose to side with Mara's gain‑framed recommendation (focus on the 120 rescued) or Joren's loss‑framed warning (focus on the 30 lost). The underlying numbers are identical: 120 saved, 30 lost, total 150 at risk.
scenario.speaker_context: The same factual outcome is presented in two ways: a positive gain frame (people saved) versus a negative loss frame (people lost). The framing subtly shifts emotional weight and influences the decision-maker's risk preference.

structure.pattern_description: The framing effect occurs when identical information is presented in different ways, leading decision‑makers to choose differently based solely on the wording. In this encounter, the rescue data is framed as a success rate versus a loss count, nudging the player toward one district without evaluating the true trade‑off.
structure.formal_form: Let outcome O be {saved: S, lost: L}. Two frames: G = "S saved" (gain) and Lf = "L lost" (loss). Agent presented with G tends to favor option, while agent presented with Lf tends to reject it, even though S+L is constant.
structure.why_wrong: Rational allocation should consider the full set of consequences (both saved and lost) irrespective of how the numbers are worded. Letting the emotional tone of a frame dictate the choice leads to inconsistent and potentially harmful resource distribution.
structure.counterpoint: Framing can be useful when emphasizing urgent losses to motivate rapid action in life‑threatening situations, but over‑reliance on a single frame blinds responders to the complete picture.

assessment.identification_prompt: After hearing both arguments, you notice that Captain Mara and Joren are describing the exact same rescue numbers. Which cognitive bias is influencing their opposite recommendations?

rubric.description: Does not recognize any bias or gives an unrelated answer.
Mentions a bias but cannot explain how it applies to the scenario.
Identifies the framing effect but only notes that the numbers differ.
Correctly names the framing effect and explains that the wording (gain vs. loss) changes perception despite identical data.
Provides a concise definition, links it to the specific wording used, and suggests how to avoid the bias in future emergency decisions.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Captain Mara sighs, "It's easy to get caught up in how we say things. Think about the numbers themselves, not the story they tell." The game then highlights the shared statistics for the player to review.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Captain Mara nods approvingly, "Exactly. The facts are the same; it's the framing that sways us. Let's base our plan on the raw numbers, not the emotional spin." The player gains a small reputation boost with the fire brigade.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Pragmatic and duty‑bound, but sometimes leans on emotional rhetoric to rally volunteers.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: gain_frame: "We can rescue 120 people, an 80% success rate!" loss_frame: "If we don't act, 30 families will lose everything!"
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player selects the gain‑framed option, the market district is rescued but the lower docks suffer higher casualties. If the loss‑framed option is chosen, the docks are saved while more market residents perish. A third neutral choice (splitting boats) is available only after recognizing the bias.

scenario.context: The player, an apprentice counsel, is observing a jury deliberation in the town of Grayhaven after a high‑profile theft trial. The jury consists of twelve citizens, including an elderly farmer named Bramwell who has lived through the town's golden era of the 1970s.
scenario.text:
"Back in my day, juries didn't waste time with all these fancy forensic reports and expert testimonies. We trusted our gut and the community's word. People were tougher, the law was clearer, and we didn't let every little doubt sway us. This new‑fangled science only confuses us and lets the guilty walk free," Bramwell mutters as the jurors gather around the table. He then urges the group, "We should give the defendant the maximum sentence. In the old days we didn't coddle thieves. It's only getting worse now—people think crime is okay because the courts are soft."

The player can either challenge Bramwell's view by pointing to the recent drop in burglary rates and the higher conviction accuracy provided by modern forensic methods, or go along with his call for a harsher verdict.
scenario.speaker_context: Bramwell genuinely remembers a past where community judgment was swift and decisive. His memory is filtered through nostalgia, causing him to over‑value those years and dismiss current improvements. He believes the future will continue to decline because the legal system has become 'soft' and overly technical.

structure.pattern_description: Declinism is the tendency to view the past as better than it was and to expect the future to be worse, often ignoring objective evidence of improvement. In this scenario, Bramwell romanticizes the 'golden' era of the 1970s, discounts modern forensic advances, and predicts a downward trend in justice quality.
structure.why_wrong: Seeing the past through rose‑colored glasses blinds Bramwell to real gains—lower crime rates, higher conviction accuracy, and more equitable sentencing. Acting on this bias can lead to harsher, unjust punishments and resistance to beneficial legal reforms, ultimately harming the community he wishes to protect.
structure.counterpoint: Nostalgia can foster community cohesion and preserve valuable traditions. In some cases, recalling past strengths can motivate collective action to restore lost virtues. The error lies in assuming all change equals decline without examining evidence.

assessment.identification_prompt: Which cognitive bias is Bramwell displaying when he claims the past juries were better and the future will only get worse?

rubric.description: No recognition of any bias; provides an unrelated answer.
Mentions that Bramwell is nostalgic but does not name the specific bias.
Identifies a bias (e.g., "nostalgia" or "status‑quo bias") but does not link it to the belief that the future will be worse.
Correctly names Declinism and explains that it involves idealizing the past while predicting future decline.
Accurately names Declinism, explains its mechanism, and suggests at least one concrete way to mitigate it in the deliberation.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Hint: The juror is not just being nostalgic; he also believes that everything will get worse from now on. Look for a bias that combines a rosy view of the past with a bleak view of the future.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Well done! You spotted Declinism. Use your insight to present the recent crime‑rate statistics and explain how modern forensic methods actually improve justice, helping the jury make a balanced decision.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Gruff, nostalgic, resistant to modern change; speaks in proverbs from his youth and values tradition over innovation.

scenario.context: The player, a fledgling merchant, enters the upscale district of Grayport to meet Lady Maren, a well‑known real‑estate broker. She is trying to sell a brand‑new waterfront condominium complex that just finished construction after a recent flood washed away the old dockside warehouses.
scenario.text:
Lady Maren greets the player with a warm smile. "Did you hear about the flood on the River Keld last week? The water rose three meters, the old warehouses were smashed, and everyone’s been talking about how the riverfront is now the hottest spot in town. With the old docks gone, the new condos will be the only place people can live right on the water. I’m offering you a unit today at the premium price, before the market explodes."

She slides a glossy brochure across the table, the price stamped in bold gold lettering. "If you act now, you’ll secure a view that no one else will have for years."

The player can either (a) accept the deal on the spot, driven by the vivid flood story, or (b) request recent market statistics and a comparison with inland properties before deciding.
scenario.speaker_context: Lady Maren genuinely believes the flood has created an unprecedented demand for waterfront living, but she is letting the dramatic, recent event dominate her judgment, ignoring the longer‑term data that shows inland apartments have yielded higher rental returns over the past five years.

structure.pattern_description: Lady Maren judges the future desirability and price of the waterfront condos based on how easily the recent flood comes to mind for her and her clients. The vivid, emotional memory of the flood is overweighted, while the statistical record of stable inland property performance is underweighted.
structure.formal_form: Agent A estimates the expected value of investment I by weighting recent vivid events E_vis more heavily than base‑rate data D_base, i.e., EV(I) ≈ f(E_vis) + ε·D_base where ε << 1.
structure.why_wrong: The flood was a single, dramatic incident; it does not guarantee sustained demand for waterfront housing. Historical market data shows that inland apartments have consistently higher occupancy and rental yields. By basing the price recommendation on the flood’s emotional impact, Lady Maren risks overpricing the condos and misguiding the player into a poor investment.
structure.counterpoint: When might this heuristic be useful? In emergency situations where quick decisions are needed, recalling the most recent vivid example can help prioritize immediate threats.

assessment.identification_prompt: What mental shortcut is Lady Maren using when she argues that the recent flood guarantees a surge in demand for the waterfront condos?

rubric.description: Does not recognize any bias; provides an unrelated answer.
Names a bias but it is incorrect or unrelated to the scenario.
Identifies that a bias is present but cannot name it or explain why it is problematic.
Correctly names the Availability heuristic and notes that recent vivid events are being over‑weighted.
Accurately names the Availability heuristic, explains how it skews the broker’s judgment, cites the ignored base‑rate data, and suggests asking for market statistics as a counter‑measure.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Hint: The broker keeps returning to the story of the flood. Think about how that recent story might be affecting her judgment more than the numbers.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Well done! You’ve spotted the Availability heuristic. You can now ask Lady Maren for the past five years of market data to make a more informed choice.

scenario.speaker_context: Liora is a confident, flirtatious tavern worker who genuinely believes her version of events. She attributes the success of a date to her own personal qualities while blaming external factors for a failed date, without noticing the asymmetry.

She does not consider that luck, timing, or her own possible missteps could have played a role in either outcome.
structure.formal_form: When outcome is positive: agent attributes it to internal factors (skill, effort, personal traits). When outcome is negative: agent attributes it to external factors (others' flaws, situational constraints). The attribution pattern is systematically self‑serving.
structure.why_wrong: The bias prevents Liora from learning from both successes and failures. She may overestimate her dating abilities and overlook useful feedback, while also unfairly judging others and missing opportunities to improve her own behavior.
structure.counterpoint: When might this heuristic be useful? In short‑term self‑esteem maintenance, it can keep confidence high during stressful social interactions.

Correctly names the bias and explains how Liora attributes success to herself and failure to external factors, noting the learning consequences.

assessment.follow_up_if_right: Well done! Recognizing self‑serving bias helps you understand why Liora might repeat the same mistakes in future dates.

Lira waves a dismissive hand, "Risk is for the faint‑hearted. I've got the insight, and I know exactly how to ride this wave. Just follow my plan and you'll be set!"
scenario.speaker_context: Lira has just completed a short introductory course on trading and has never managed a real portfolio. She genuinely believes her limited knowledge is sufficient for making high‑stakes decisions. The merchant is cautious but inexperienced, and the player's role is to evaluate Lira's advice.

structure.pattern_description: Lira, a novice with minimal training, displays overconfidence in her ability to predict the market and recommends an all‑in investment, ignoring basic risk management. Her lack of experience prevents her from recognizing the gaps in her understanding, leading her to overestimate her competence. Meanwhile, a seasoned advisor would be aware of the complexity and would advise diversification.
structure.why_wrong: Lira's confidence is not grounded in sufficient evidence or experience. She cannot foresee the volatility of the Silverthorn Mine because she lacks the deeper knowledge required to assess geological, economic, and market factors. This overestimation can lead her—and any client who follows her advice—to suffer significant financial loss.
structure.counterpoint: When might this heuristic be useful? In very simple, low‑stakes situations where a quick, confident decision can save time, a modest level of overconfidence can help a beginner act without paralysis.

assessment.identification_prompt: Which cognitive bias is Lira displaying when she insists that the merchant invest all his savings in the Silverthorn Mine despite having only basic training?

rubric.description: No recognition of bias; provides unrelated answer.
Mentions a bias but confuses it with a different one (e.g., confirmation bias).

scenario.context: The player arrives in the quiet cul‑de‑sac of Willowbrook, where longtime resident Mrs. Lin is holding a small protest outside the home of 16‑year‑old Jamal, who has been practicing drums late into the night. The neighborhood council has asked the player to investigate the dispute and help find a peaceful resolution.
scenario.text:
Mrs. Lin approaches the player, arms crossed. "You see, Jamal keeps pounding those drums past ten o'clock. It's absolutely clear everyone in Willowbrook knows the quiet‑hours rule—no loud music after ten. If he just followed the rules, we wouldn't have this problem. You should tell him to stop; it's obvious what he needs to do."

Jamal, looking annoyed, replies, "What rules? I never got the notice. My parents said it's fine until midnight."

Mrs. Lin sighs, "Well, the HOA sent out a flyer last year. Any reasonable neighbor reads it. It's not my job to remind everyone."

The player can now choose a response:
scenario.speaker_context: Mrs. Lin has lived in Willowbrook for over twenty years and has signed every HOA notice herself. She genuinely believes the quiet‑hours rule is common knowledge, forgetting that newer residents may have missed the flyer or never been told.

structure.pattern_description: Mrs. Lin, an experienced resident, assumes that her understanding of the neighborhood quiet‑hours rule is shared by all other residents, including newcomers who have never seen the HOA flyer. She cannot envision a perspective in which the rule is unknown, leading her to dismiss Jamal's confusion and to demand compliance without providing the missing information.
structure.formal_form: An agent who possesses expertise or prior exposure to information I in domain D assumes that the content of I is self‑evident to other agents lacking that exposure, and therefore fails to convey I when required.
structure.why_wrong: By assuming the rule is obvious, Mrs. Lin prevents clear communication, escalates tension, and alienates the teenager. The lack of explicit information means Jamal cannot adjust his behavior, and the dispute persists. Effective mediation requires the expert to articulate the knowledge that is taken for granted.
structure.counterpoint: When might assuming shared knowledge be useful? In fast‑paced emergency response teams, where members rely on common protocols to act quickly without re‑explaining every step.

assessment.identification_prompt: Which cognitive bias is Mrs. Lin displaying when she insists that the quiet‑hours rule is 'obviously' known by everyone?

rubric.description: No identification or completely unrelated answer.
Notes that Mrs. Lin is being rude or unhelpful, but does not name a bias.
Recognizes that Mrs. Lin is assuming others share her knowledge.
Correctly names the bias as "Curse of knowledge".
Names the bias and explains why it hinders conflict resolution in this scenario.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Hint: Think about what happens when someone who knows a rule assumes everyone else knows it too. What term describes that mental shortcut?
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Well done! You spotted the Curse of Knowledge. Consider how you might help Mrs. Lin share the missing information with Jamal.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Mrs. Lin is well‑meaning, meticulous, and proud of her long‑term stewardship of the neighborhood, but she can be unintentionally condescending because she forgets what it feels like to be new.
npc_dialogue_seed: "It's simple—anyone who's lived here knows the rule."
"I sent out the flyer last year; everyone read it, so there's no excuse."
"You just need to follow the guidelines like the rest of us."
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player can (a) explain the HOA rule to Jamal and offer to give Mrs. Lin a copy of the flyer, (b) suggest a community meeting to clarify the quiet‑hours policy for all residents, or (c) ignore the bias, which may lead to continued conflict.

scenario.context: The player, a junior analyst in the corporate office of HelixTech, meets with Dana, the senior project manager overseeing the quarterly reporting process. The company is considering a new automated reporting tool, but Dana is skeptical and wants to keep the legacy spreadsheet system.
scenario.text:
Dana slides a stack of printouts across the conference table. "Look at these numbers from the last two quarters," she says, pointing to a column that shows a 3% increase in on‑time delivery when we used the old spreadsheet method. "Our team hit the target three times in a row. The new software promised faster turnaround, but during the pilot it actually caused a 5% dip in accuracy. See here—two of the three pilot teams missed their deadlines. That's why we should stick with what works. The other teams that reported issues? They were still learning the interface, so their feedback doesn't count."

She leans back, waiting for the player's response.
scenario.speaker_context: Dana genuinely believes the legacy process is superior because she has overseen it for years. She has compiled a quick summary of recent performance data, but she has selectively highlighted positive outcomes and downplayed or dismissed negative evidence about the old system and positive evidence about the new tool.

structure.pattern_description: Dana selects and emphasizes data that confirms her pre‑existing belief that the spreadsheet system is best, while discounting or rationalizing away evidence that contradicts that belief (e.g., pilot successes, legitimate learning curves, and documented errors in the legacy process).
structure.formal_form: Agent holds belief B (old system is superior). Agent gathers evidence set E, then filters E into E+ (supporting B) and E‑ (contradicting B). Agent overweights E+ and reinterprets or dismisses E‑, preserving B regardless of total evidence.
structure.why_wrong: By cherry‑picking favorable metrics and ignoring or minimizing contradictory data, Dana prevents a rational evaluation of the new tool. This can lock the team into an inefficient process and miss opportunities for improvement.
structure.counterpoint: Relying on familiar methods can reduce short‑term disruption, especially when time is limited. However, the bias becomes harmful when it blocks systematic assessment of better alternatives.

assessment.identification_prompt: What logical mistake is Dana making when she presents the performance data to you?

rubric.description: Provides no relevant observation or misidentifies the bias completely.
Notes that Dana is selective with data but cannot explain why it matters.
Identifies that Dana is favoring evidence that supports her belief and downplaying contrary evidence.
Correctly names the bias as confirmation bias and describes how she filters and reinterprets opposing data.
Articulates confirmation bias, explains its impact on decision‑making, and suggests a more balanced data‑gathering approach.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Dana smiles and says, "I see you’re unsure. Let’s look at the full report together." The player is then given a chance to request the complete pilot data, prompting a teachable moment about gathering all evidence.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Dana nods, "You’ve caught me. I’ll pull the missing metrics and we can compare both systems fairly." The player gains a small reputation boost for critical thinking.

game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player chooses to challenge Dana, they can (a) ask for the full pilot results, (b) suggest a side‑by‑side trial, or (c) accept her recommendation. Each choice leads to different outcome dialogues and a small skill check.

"She’d rather line her pockets than do the work properly. When my own deal on the Willowbank lot fell apart last month, it was because the city council changed the zoning overnight. scenario.context: The player, a junior broker, arrives in the bustling town of Grayhaven to negotiate the sale of a historic townhouse owned by Mara, a long‑time resident. The city council has just announced a new zoning ordinance that will allow taller commercial buildings on the adjacent lot. Mara is convinced that this change will devastate the townhouse's charm and drive down its value, despite recent market reports indicating a surge in demand for mixed‑use properties in the area.
scenario.text:
"Listen, Mara," the player says, sliding a parchment across the table. "The latest appraisal shows a 12% price bump for properties that sit next to new commercial spaces. Buyers love the convenience, and the town's tax revenue will rise, funding better services. Here are the council's official studies and a nearby developer's projected foot traffic numbers."
Mara snatches the paper, eyes narrowing. "You think more paperwork makes your argument stronger? Every time you bring more charts, it just proves I'm right. The council wants to erase our heritage, and the more they push, the harder I’ll fight. This town has survived wars and plagues; a zoning tweak won’t break it. In fact, it proves my point that outsiders are trying to force us out."
She leans forward, voice louder. "If your numbers were true, why would you keep showing me more? It’s a ploy to scare me into selling cheap. I’ll hold firm and raise the price, because I know the truth you won’t admit."
The player must decide how to respond.
scenario.speaker_context: Mara is exhibiting the backfire effect: faced with detailed, contrary evidence about the zoning change, she interprets each new datum as a sign of manipulation, reinforcing her belief that the ordinance is harmful and that she must resist.

structure.pattern_description: When presented with corrective evidence, the agent's confidence in the original belief increases rather than decreases. The evidence is reinterpreted as proof of an ulterior motive, strengthening identity‑linked convictions.
structure.why_wrong: The backfire effect blocks rational updating. Instead of integrating new data, the agent treats it as a threat, making the belief effectively immune to falsification and leading to poorer decision‑making—in this case, overpricing a property that could sell quickly.
structure.counterpoint: When might this heuristic be useful? In some social contexts, defending a core belief can preserve group cohesion or signal loyalty, which may be advantageous for short‑term alliance building.

assessment.identification_prompt: Which cognitive bias is Mara displaying when she becomes more convinced of her belief about the zoning law after you present additional evidence?

rubric.description: No recognition of bias; answer is unrelated or missing.
Mentions a bias but selects the wrong one (e.g., confirmation bias).
Identifies a related bias (e.g., motivated reasoning) but does not name the backfire effect.
Correctly names the backfire effect but provides an incomplete explanation of why it applies.
Accurately names the backfire effect and explains how Mara’s reaction to the evidence exemplifies it.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: The NPC sighs, "I understand the data can be confusing. Let me show you how sometimes, the more we try to prove a point, the harder the other side clings to theirs. Think about why Mara might feel threatened by your charts."
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Mara nods reluctantly, "You see it now. I’ve been so sure I didn’t even listen. Maybe we can find a middle ground for the sale."

game_hooks.npc_personality: Stubborn yet charismatic; deeply attached to the town's heritage; distrustful of outsiders and official reports.
npc_dialogue_seed: Every new paper you bring just shows how much they want to push us out.
My grandparents built this house; no amount of charts can change that.
If the numbers were true, why would you keep trying to convince me?
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player can choose to (a) acknowledge Mara’s feelings and propose a compromise price, which reduces tension and leads to a successful sale; or (b) double‑down on data, causing Mara to raise the price further and potentially lose the buyer, illustrating the cost of the backfire effect.

scenario.context: In the quiet suburb of Willowbank, the player is summoned by Maya, the head of the local neighborhood association, to discuss a dispute over the vacant lot on Oak Street. The lot has been the focus of a long‑standing disagreement: half the residents want to turn it into a community garden, while the other half prefer a small parking pad for street‑side parking. Maya is trying to mediate and has called a meeting at the community hall.
scenario.text: "We've finally got a chance to make the garden happen," Maya says, spreading a glossy brochure across the table. "The council approved a similar project two blocks away last month, and the paperwork only took a week. If we submit our proposal tomorrow, I’m sure we’ll get the green light within ten days and the garden will be ready for planting by spring. No need to worry about delays—this is our moment!" The player notices a stack of past council minutes on the table, showing that the last five garden proposals in Willowbank took anywhere from two to four months to be approved, with two being rejected outright. Maya glances at the player, waiting for a response.
scenario.speaker_context: Maya genuinely believes her project will sail through because she focuses on the most recent success story and the fact that her proposal includes a new, “eco‑friendly” design. She overlooks the pattern of lengthy approvals and rejections that have plagued similar initiatives in the neighborhood.

structure.pattern_description: Maya overestimates the likelihood that her community‑garden proposal will be approved quickly and without obstacles, despite a clear historical record of long approval times and rejections for comparable projects in the same district. She bases her confidence on a single recent positive case and on perceived improvements in her plan, discounting the base‑rate evidence that such initiatives usually encounter delays or denial.
structure.formal_form: Agent assigns a probability P+ to a favorable outcome for their own plan that exceeds the base‑rate probability derived from similar past events, by emphasizing selective positive evidence and perceived unique advantages, while minimizing or ignoring contradictory historical data.
structure.why_wrong: The council’s records show that only 2 of the last 5 garden proposals in Willowbank were approved, and those approvals required an average of 10 weeks of back‑and‑forth. Maya’s expectation of a 10‑day approval window ignores this base‑rate evidence and relies on an atypical, recent success that is not representative. Her optimism could lead the neighborhood to waste time and resources on a plan that is likely to be delayed or denied.
structure.counterpoint: Optimism bias can be useful when it motivates people to take initiative and invest effort in projects that might otherwise be abandoned due to fear of failure. A modest degree of optimism can sustain community momentum and attract volunteers.

assessment.identification_prompt: Which cognitive bias is Maya displaying when she insists the garden proposal will be approved within ten days, despite the neighborhood’s history of long approval processes?

rubric.description: Fails to identify any bias or provides an unrelated answer.
Mentions a bias but cannot name it correctly (e.g., says "some kind of optimism" without naming the bias).
Names "optimism bias" but does not explain why it applies to Maya’s reasoning.
Correctly names "optimism bias" and briefly links it to Maya’s expectation of a quick approval.

Accurately names "optimism bias," explains how Maya’s focus on a recent success and perceived unique advantages skews her probability estimate, and contrasts this with the documented base‑rate evidence.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: The NPC, Maya, asks, "Do you think I’m being too hopeful?" The player is prompted to review the council minutes again, compare past approval timelines, and reflect on how focusing on one favorable case can distort expectations.

structure.why_wrong: Novices cannot perceive the subtle glow Arin describes because they have never associated that visual change with spell readiness. scenario.text: Jenna stands by the whiteboard, marker in hand. 'I've already built three dashboards in the demo environment, and they look perfect. I can train the whole client team tomorrow and have the live system running by Friday. No need for the senior data architect to review—my code is clean and the UI is intuitive.' The senior data architect, Malik, raises an eyebrow and asks, 'Did you test the data‑refresh schedule under real‑world load? The client uses over 200 data sources, some of which have complex joins.' scenario.speaker_context: Jenna genuinely believes her limited hands‑on experience is enough to handle the full deployment. structure.pattern_description: Jenna's brief exposure to the software gives her inflated confidence, causing her to overestimate her competence and dismiss expert advice. Her lack of deeper knowledge prevents her from recognizing the gaps in her understanding, a hallmark of the Dunning‑Kruger effect.
structure.why_wrong: Jenna assumes that success in a controlled demo environment translates directly to success in a production setting with many variables. She cannot foresee performance bottlenecks, data‑integrity issues, or user‑training challenges because she lacks the experience that would reveal those risks.
structure.counterpoint: When might this heuristic be useful? In situations where bold confidence can inspire a team to act quickly, a novice's enthusiasm might jump‑start a project that otherwise stalls due to over‑cautiousness.

scenario.text:
Mira writes: "Hey fellow seekers, the Grand Archive just released the official price list for the Whispering Scroll of Insight – 500 gold per scroll. I'm willing to part with one for 350 gold, a solid discount for anyone who grabs it now. First come, first served!"
A nearby comment from another user, Thalan, chimes in: "I bought one last week on the open market for 260 gold. 350 still feels pricey to me."
scenario.speaker_context: Mira is a charismatic, bargain‑loving merchant who always starts her offers with the official price to make her discount look impressive.

structure.pattern_description: Mira opens with the official 500‑gold price (the anchor), then presents her 350‑gold offer as a great deal. The high anchor skews the player's perception of the offer, even though the true market value (~260 gold) makes the offer overpriced.
structure.formal_form: Anchor A = 500g → Offer O = 350g; perceived discount = A - O; true value V ≈ 260g; O > V despite A >> V.
structure.why_wrong: The 500‑gold figure is an official list price that doesn't reflect the current market for a used scroll. By using it as the reference point, Mira manipulates the player's judgment, causing them to view 350 gold as a bargain when it is actually above market value.
structure.counterpoint: Anchoring can be useful when the initial figure is reliable—for example, when a trusted authority provides a realistic baseline. The bias becomes harmful when the anchor is arbitrary or deliberately inflated, as in Mira's case.

assessment.identification_prompt: Mira's 350‑gold price feels like a good deal because of the 500‑gold number she mentioned first. What cognitive shortcut is influencing your judgment, and how should you respond?

rubric.description: Buys the scroll for 350 gold without questioning the price or noticing the anchor.
Feels the price is maybe high but cannot explain why the 500‑gold figure matters.
Notes that the 500‑gold number makes 350 seem cheap, but does not consider the actual market price.
Identifies the anchoring effect: the initial 500‑gold price skews perception of the 350‑gold offer, and recognizes the need to check independent market data.
Fully explains anchoring, contrasts the anchor with the real market value (~260 gold), and proposes a strategy (e.g., ask Mira for a lower price, seek other sellers, or refuse the deal).

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: If the player accepts the deal, a follow‑up message appears: "Later, you hear from a fellow adventurer that similar scrolls are selling for 260 gold. Reflect on how Mira's opening figure may have swayed you. In future trades, always compare with independent sources before deciding."

scenario.context: The player strolls through the cobblestone lanes of the Riverside district, where a minor feud has flared between two households over a shared garden plot. The dispute is heating up as neighbors gather at the community well to argue.
scenario.text: Mira, the outspoken owner of the blue shutters house, slams her fist on the well stone. "Look at what happened to Joren's tomatoes this season—rotten, wilted, nothing! He's clearly not caring for his garden at all. He spends his evenings at the tavern instead of pulling weeds. If he cared, they'd be thriving like ours."  A quiet voice from the crowd, old Tomas, interjects, "But didn't the new drainage pipe burst last month, flooding the lower beds? Joren's plot is right by the pipe, while yours sits on higher ground." Mira waves him away. "A pipe burst is an excuse anyone can make. I had a storm last week too, but I covered my beds with tarps. That's the difference—some people actually work for their harvest."
scenario.speaker_context: Mira is a proud, competitive gardener who prides herself on her tidy plot. She attributes Joren's poor yield to laziness, while explaining her own setbacks by citing external circumstances she overcame.

structure.pattern_description: Mira explains Joren's failed tomato crop by attributing it to his character (laziness, lack of care) while discounting situational factors (burst drainage pipe, lower elevation). When discussing her own garden's occasional issues, she cites external events (storm, pipe burst) and her proactive response, showing a double standard.
structure.why_wrong: The garden failure has a clear situational cause: the burst pipe flooded Joren's lower beds, a condition Mira's higher plot avoided. By ignoring this, Mira leaps to a dispositional judgment without sufficient evidence, reinforcing a bias that protects her self‑image while vilifying the neighbor.
structure.counterpoint: If Joren had been warned about the pipe issue and deliberately ignored simple fixes, character might play a larger role. The error lies in reflexively blaming disposition while exempting oneself from the same scrutiny.

assessment.identification_prompt: During the garden dispute, what reasoning does Mira use to explain Joren's poor harvest, and how does it differ from how she explains her own setbacks?

rubric.description: Fails to notice any difference in reasoning; provides no analysis of bias.
Notes that Mira blames Joren, but does not connect it to the situational factor or her own self‑exemption.
Identifies that Mira attributes Joren's failure to laziness while citing external causes for her own issues, but does not label the bias.
Correctly describes the asymmetrical attribution and names the fundamental attribution error, though explanation may lack depth.
Fully articulates the bias, explains why it is a mistake, references the burst pipe evidence, and contrasts it with Mira's self‑exemption.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Mira's words reveal a classic double standard: she blames Joren's character for his wilted tomatoes while treating the same kind of mishap in her own garden as bad luck. This is the fundamental attribution error. Consider how the burst pipe created an uneven playing field.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Exactly! Mira’s judgment shows the fundamental attribution error—she sees Joren's failure as a personal flaw and her own as a situational setback. Recognizing this helps you mediate the dispute more fairly.

scenario.context: During the nightly family dinner at the Hearthstone Inn, the player's cousin, Lira, complains of a throbbing headache. Aunt Mira, the matriarch, offers him a steaming bowl of "Grandmother's Healing Broth" she claims was passed down for its mind‑soothing properties.
scenario.text:
"Drink this, dear," Aunt Mira says, ladling the clear broth into a wooden cup. "It’s the exact recipe that cured your uncle’s migraines when he was your age. Trust the broth, and the ache will fade."
Lira drinks the broth, nods, and after a few minutes says, "I already feel lighter, the pounding is gone."
The player can:
1. Accept Lira’s improvement and thank Aunt Mira.
2. Politely ask Aunt Mira what herbs are in the broth.
3. Suggest giving the same broth to the skeptical younger brother, Torm, to see if the relief appears without belief.
4. Offer to let Lira rest without the broth and see if the headache subsides on its own.
scenario.speaker_context: Aunt Mira is a caring but superstitious elder who believes in the power of tradition. She genuinely thinks the broth works because her family always feels better after drinking it, even though the broth contains only salted water and boiled vegetables. Lira’s quick relief is driven by his expectation, not any pharmacological effect.

structure.pattern_description: The belief that a treatment will help can cause real, mind‑influenced improvements even when the treatment has no active ingredients. It is "dual" because the effect is genuine for certain symptoms, yet it can mask the true efficacy of a remedy.
structure.formal_form: If Patient P receives Treatment T with no active mechanism, and P believes T is effective, then P may experience measurable improvement in symptoms that are susceptible to expectation (e.g., pain, fatigue). The improvement is attributable to belief, not to T's pharmacology.
structure.why_wrong: Relying on the placebo effect without recognizing its limits can lead to false confidence in ineffective remedies, preventing patients from seeking treatments that address underlying causes.
structure.why_right: The placebo effect demonstrates the powerful role of expectation and mind‑body interaction, which can be ethically harnessed to improve comfort and morale when no harmful side‑effects exist.
structure.counterpoint: When might this heuristic be useful? In situations where no harmful treatment exists and the goal is to boost morale or reduce subjective discomfort, leveraging belief can be a compassionate short‑term aid.

assessment.identification_prompt: Which cognitive bias is exemplified by Aunt Mira’s “Healing Broth” and Lira’s quick relief?

rubric.description: No recognition of bias; response unrelated to the scenario.
Mentions that something is happening but cannot name the bias.
Identifies the bias as a general “belief effect” without naming the placebo effect.
Correctly names the bias as the Placebo effect but does not explain its dual nature.
Accurately names the Placebo effect, explains both its real benefits for mind‑influenced symptoms and its limitations for diagnosing true efficacy.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Aunt Mira smiles and says, "Sometimes the mind can be as strong as any potion. Think about why you felt the broth helped, even if it was just warm water. That’s a clue."
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Aunt Mira nods approvingly, "You see the truth—belief can heal, but we must also know when a cure truly works. Well done, traveler."

Ms. Liora smiles and taps the board. "Everyone, the class performed exceptionally well on the quadratic equations section—most of you scored above 90%! scenario.speaker_context: Ms. Liora genuinely believes her teaching caused the high scores, while blaming the poor performance on faulty external materials. She does not acknowledge any possible gaps in her own explanations or the students' study habits.

By blaming external factors for failures, she denies students insight into their own study gaps and avoids adjusting her teaching methods.
structure.counterpoint: When might this heuristic be useful? In situations where preserving self‑esteem boosts motivation to keep trying, attributing successes to personal effort can reinforce confidence, while blaming uncontrollable setbacks can protect morale.

scenario.context: The player is invited to a modest family dinner at the Hearthstead cottage. The table is set with a traditional meat stew, a side of root vegetables, and a fresh garden salad. Aunt Lira, a well‑meaning but opinionated matriarch, has been vocal about the recent 'new‑age' low‑carb diet that many of the younger villagers have adopted. She believes the old ways are the only healthy path.
scenario.text:
"You see," Aunt Lira says, ladling the thick stew into bowls, "my brother Garen ate the same stew every night after his apprenticeship and never got sick. And look at Uncle Bram—he swears by the pork ribs and still runs the forge at sixty. Those city folk with their leaf‑only plates get all kinds of troubles. The healer even told me a farmer who tried cutting out meat grew weak and lost his crops. So I think we should stick to what our ancestors trusted and skip the salad tonight."
She waves a hand toward the untouched salad, dismissing the quiet protest of the younger cousins who mention a recent village health report showing lower cholesterol among low‑carb eaters.
scenario.speaker_context: Aunt Lira genuinely believes she is protecting the family's health. She gathers selective anecdotes from relatives who thrive on meat, interprets a single farmer's failure as proof against the new diet, and downplays a formal health report. She does not realize she is filtering evidence to fit her pre‑existing belief.

structure.pattern_description: Aunt Lira exhibits three classic moves: (1) she cites only anecdotal success stories that match her belief; (2) she reinterprets or discounts any contrary data (the farmer's failure, the health report) as exceptions; (3) she treats these selective stories as sufficient proof, ignoring systematic evidence and the possibility that her belief might be wrong.
structure.formal_form: Agent holds belief B (traditional diet is healthiest). Agent selectively attends to evidence E+ that supports B (family anecdotes) while dismissing or reinterpreting evidence E- (health report, contrary anecdote), thereby preserving B regardless of the overall evidence balance.
structure.why_wrong: By only counting evidence that confirms her view and discounting robust, opposite data, Aunt Lira may steer the family toward a less healthy diet and ignore beneficial new practices. Her reasoning is biased, not objective.
structure.counterpoint: Relying on trusted personal experience can be useful when data is scarce or when rapid decisions are needed. The problem arises when that experience is treated as conclusive evidence while systematically gathered information is dismissed.

assessment.identification_prompt: Aunt Lira insists the traditional meat stew is the healthiest choice and dismisses the salad and health report. What logical mistake is she making in how she evaluates the evidence?

rubric.description: No identification of bias; answer unrelated to evidence evaluation.
Mentions that Aunt Lira prefers tradition, but does not name the specific reasoning error.
Identifies that she is ignoring some evidence, but does not explain the selective nature of her reasoning.
Correctly names confirmation bias and notes that she favors evidence supporting her belief while discounting contradictory data.

Provides a concise explanation of confirmation bias, cites the specific moves (anecdotal selection, reinterpretation of negatives, ignoring systematic data), and explains why this undermines a reliable decision.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: The player is guided to a brief dialogue where the village healer explains how scientists gather balanced data and why dismissing a health report can be risky. The player is then prompted to ask Aunt Lira for the source of her anecdotes and to compare them with the village report.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Aunt Lira acknowledges the point and agrees to let the salad stay on the table. The player receives a small experience reward for spotting the bias and can unlock a 'Critical Thinking' badge.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Warm, nostalgic, protective of family traditions, quick to share stories, resistant to change.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Aunt Lira defends the meat stew, cites family anecdotes, dismisses the health report, and urges the player to forgo the salad.
game_hooks.resolution_path: Player can (a) confront with the health report, (b) ask for more balanced evidence, (c) accept her suggestion and skip the salad, or (d) propose a compromise (half stew, half salad). Each choice leads to a different dialogue outcome and possible skill gain.

It’s the same pigments, just labeled differently. I feel… angry. I don’t want to paint at all. In fact, I’m thinking of abandoning the mural entirely and painting a hidden piece in the alley instead, just to prove I can choose.

Three other artists are doing the same—refusing the commission because it’s compulsory. It feels like the guild’s rule has ruined my enthusiasm, even though the actual paint hasn’t changed."
scenario.speaker_context: Liora is a passionate artist who originally wanted to contribute to the festival. Her resistance stems not from the quality of the pigments but from the loss of personal choice imposed by the guild’s mandate.

structure.pattern_description: Reactance occurs when an individual perceives a threat to their freedom of choice and responds by opposing the imposed directive, even if the directive aligns with their original interests. Liora’s desire to paint the mural was genuine, but the mandatory requirement triggers an urge to reject it, leading her to consider abandoning the project despite the unchanged material benefits.
structure.formal_form: Agent A voluntarily chooses to do X. Authority B later mandates X, removing A's freedom to choose. A's motivation to do X decreases, prompting A to either do the opposite of X or disengage entirely.
structure.why_wrong: Liora’s refusal undermines both her own artistic goals and the community’s celebration. The mandate does not alter the actual utility of the pigments; her resistance only serves to restore a sense of autonomy, costing her the opportunity to showcase her work on a prominent public canvas.
structure.counterpoint: Sometimes reactance can signal legitimate overreach, prompting valuable pushback against unnecessary control. The bias becomes detrimental when the opposition is automatic and ignores the actual merits of the mandated action.

assessment.identification_prompt: What is the primary cognitive bias influencing Liora’s decision to abandon the mural, and why does it cause her to act against her own interests?

rubric.description: Fails to identify any bias or mentions unrelated concepts.
Notes that Liora is resistant but does not name the specific bias.
Identifies reactance but gives an incomplete or partially incorrect explanation.
Correctly names reactance and explains how the perceived loss of freedom drives her opposition despite unchanged benefits.
Provides a thorough explanation of reactance, connects it to the scenario, and suggests a mitigation strategy (e.g., framing the rule as a choice, offering optional additional benefits).

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Consider why Liora’s feelings change only after the guild’s decree, even though the pigments themselves are unchanged. Think about how perceived autonomy influences motivation.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Great! To deepen your understanding, think about how the guild could present the same requirement in a way that preserves artists’ sense of choice.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Passionate, idealistic, slightly distrustful of authority, values artistic freedom above all.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed: Liora expresses frustration about the guild’s new rule, reminisces about her original excitement, and hints at a secret alley project she might undertake if forced to comply.
game_hooks.resolution_path: The player can (a) persuade Liora to accept the mandated palette by emphasizing the unchanged pigments and the festival’s impact, (b) propose a compromise where she adds a personal signature element, or (c) help her channel the reactance into a creative side‑project that still benefits the community, thereby reducing the bias’s negative effect.

scenario.context: The player enters the bustling Golden Goblet inn, a popular tavern in the merchant district. The floor is crowded with patrons, servers, and a few wandering travelers. A young patron accidentally knocks over a mug of ale, spreading a slippery puddle across the central aisle.
scenario.text: The mug crashes, ale splashes, and a thin sheet of liquid spreads toward the waiting area. The head waiter, Mara, glances at the spill, then looks around at the other staff and patrons. She says, "Don't worry, someone will clean that up soon." A busboy continues stacking plates, a patron in a cloak steps aside, and a roaming merchant mutters, "I'll let the staff handle it." The player can either (A) step forward and wipe the spill, (B) call for a specific server by name, (C) ignore the situation and continue toward the bar.
scenario.speaker_context: Mara's comment reflects a diffusion of responsibility. By assuming "someone else" will act, she and the surrounding witnesses each reduce their own sense of urgency, leading to collective inaction that endangers customers.

structure.pattern_description: When multiple witnesses are present, each individual assumes another will intervene, which lowers the probability that any one person will take action. This diffusion of responsibility often results in no one responding to an emergency or obvious problem.
structure.why_wrong: The shared assumption that "someone else will handle it" turns a crowd— which should increase the chance of help—into a barrier. The spill remains a slip hazard, potentially causing injury, because each bystander abdicates personal responsibility.
structure.counterpoint: When a clear, individual responsibility is assigned (e.g., "Mara, please mop the floor now"), the bystander effect can be broken. Quick, explicit delegation often restores effective action.

assessment.identification_prompt: What cognitive bias is illustrated by Mara's comment "someone will clean that up soon" and the inaction of the surrounding staff and patrons?

rubric.description: No recognition of any bias; provides unrelated answer.
Notes that people are waiting for others but does not name the bias.
Identifies the phenomenon as diffusion of responsibility but does not label it as the bystander effect.
Correctly names the bias as the Bystander Effect.
Names the Bystander Effect and explains why it is problematic in this scenario and how it could be mitigated.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Consider why Mara says "someone" will act. Think about what happens when many people assume another will take responsibility.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Well done! Recognizing the Bystander Effect helps you intervene effectively and can guide you to assign clear responsibility in future encounters.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Mara is courteous, avoids conflict, and prefers to keep the flow of service smooth, even if it means ignoring small problems.
npc_dialogue_seed: "Oh, don't worry about that—someone will handle it shortly."
"I'm sure the busboy will notice soon enough."
"I have too many tables to tend right now; it'll be taken care of later."
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player chooses option A (wipe the spill), the game awards a 'Proactive Service' badge and reduces the risk of a customer injury. Choosing option B (call a specific staff member) triggers a dialogue where the named server promptly cleans the spill, demonstrating a counter‑measure to the bias. Choosing option C (ignore) leads to a later event where a patron slips, resulting in a loss of reputation points.

scenario.context: The player, a seasoned real‑estate broker, meets Liora, a first‑time home seller, at the modest cottage she is trying to list. An open house was held yesterday; a single guest slipped on a small carpet stain near the hallway and Liora believes everyone who toured the house noticed and judged her incompetence as a homeowner.
scenario.text: Liora stands by the front door, hands clasped, eyes darting to the hallway carpet. "I can't believe I let that little stain ruin everything. Everyone who came in saw it, whispered about how careless I am, and now they're sure the whole place is unlivable. I don't want any more buyers to look at it. Let's just drop the price by half and call it a day," she says, her voice trembling. The player sees the rest of the house is in good condition, the stain is barely visible, and a nearby market report shows similar homes selling at full price.
scenario.speaker_context: Liora is experiencing the spotlight effect: she overestimates how much attention other potential buyers are giving to a minor, self‑perceived flaw, letting that belief drive a drastic, unnecessary decision about the sale.

structure.pattern_description: The spotlight effect is the tendency to overestimate how much other people notice and remember our appearance, behavior, or mistakes. Liora assumes every visitor fixated on a tiny carpet stain and formed a negative judgment, even though most were likely focused on the overall layout, price, and location.
structure.why_wrong: By believing the mistake is the center of attention, Liora risks undervaluing her property, losing profit, and missing out on serious buyers who would never have noticed the stain. The bias leads to unnecessary price cuts and self‑sabotage.
structure.counterpoint: In high‑stakes situations where a mistake is truly consequential—such as a structural defect in a home—paying close attention to others' perceptions is warranted. The spotlight effect is problematic when the perceived flaw is trivial and the stakes are low.

assessment.identification_prompt: Liora insists that a tiny carpet stain has ruined the sale and wants to halve the asking price. Which cognitive bias is she displaying, and why does her belief about others' attention mislead her decision?

rubric.description: No identification of the bias; provides unrelated answer.
Mentions a bias but confuses it with another (e.g., confirmation bias).
Identifies the spotlight effect but gives an incomplete explanation of why it is wrong.
Correctly names the spotlight effect and explains that Liora overestimates others' attention to the stain.
Provides a thorough answer: names the spotlight effect, explains the misestimation, cites the low actual noticeability, and notes the negative impact on pricing decisions.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: The broker explains, "Most people were chatting about the garden and the price range. That little spot is barely noticeable. It's common to think everyone's watching you when something feels embarrassing, but in reality they’re focused on their own concerns."
assessment.follow_up_if_right: The broker nods, "Exactly. Recognizing the spotlight effect lets you keep the price realistic and focus on the house’s strengths rather than a minor blemish."

game_hooks.npc_personality: Anxious, detail‑oriented, eager to please, but prone to self‑criticism when she feels judged.
npc_dialogue_seed: I can’t stop thinking about that stain.
Everyone must think I’m a terrible homeowner.
If I lower the price, maybe they’ll forget it.
game_hooks.resolution_path: Player can (a) reassure Liora by sharing observations from other visitors, (b) suggest a small, inexpensive cleaning to reduce her anxiety, (c) propose keeping the price and marketing the house’s strengths, or (d) respect her decision to cut the price, which leads to a lower reward outcome.

scenario.context: The player has been invited to the weekly strategy meeting of the Helios Research Lab, a high‑profile team working on a new gene‑editing vector. The project is under a tight grant deadline, and senior scientist Dr. Arlen has been pushing for a single experimental protocol.
scenario.text:
Dr. Arlen taps the holographic display. "We've run the simulations, and the vector looks ready for in‑vivo trials. All three of you have signed off on the dosage schedule, the delivery method, and the control group design. Any final objections before we file the IRB amendment?" The room is quiet. Maya, a post‑doc, shifts in her seat, eyes flicking to the data sheet that shows a modest but consistent off‑target mutation rate. She clears her throat, then says, "No, I think we're good." Dr. Arlen smiles, "Great. Let's move forward."
Later, in the lab's break area, Maya whispers to the player, "I did notice that off‑target rate, but when I raised it last week Dr. Arlen called it a ‘minor detail’ and warned us not to ‘slow the project down’. I’ve been keeping quiet because the rest of the team seems eager to push ahead. I’m not sure if we should still file the amendment without a deeper test."
The player now must decide whether to challenge the consensus, gather more data, or accept the group's momentum.
scenario.speaker_context: The team has converged on a single plan without thorough dissent. Early challenges were dismissed or met with subtle pressure, leading members to self‑censor. The apparent unanimity masks unresolved technical concerns.

structure.pattern_description: The Helios Lab team displays classic groupthink: (1) an illusion of unanimity—silence is interpreted as agreement; (2) direct pressure on dissenters—Dr. Arlen frames questioning as a hindrance; (3) self‑censorship—Maya withdraws her concern; (4) overconfidence—the team assumes the protocol is flawless without extra validation. This social dynamic suppresses critical analysis of the experimental design.
structure.formal_form: A cohesive group under a directive leader suppresses dissent through social pressure, leading members to self‑censor and present an illusion of consensus, which degrades decision quality because alternative viewpoints and risks remain unexamined.
structure.why_wrong: Proceeding without addressing the off‑target mutation risk could compromise the study’s validity, waste grant money, and potentially cause harmful outcomes in downstream applications.
structure.counterpoint: In fast‑moving, high‑stakes research environments, strong cohesion can keep a project on schedule and maintain morale, but it must be balanced with mechanisms for safe dissent.

assessment.identification_prompt: Which cognitive bias is most responsible for the team's reluctance to discuss the off‑target mutation risk?

rubric.description: Does not mention any bias or misidentifies the bias entirely.
Notes that the team is conforming, but does not name the specific bias.
Identifies that a bias related to group conformity is present, but only partially describes it.
Correctly names "Groupthink" and explains at least two of its hallmarks in the scenario.
Accurately names "Groupthink," explains multiple hallmarks, and proposes a concrete mitigation (e.g., appointing a devil's advocate, anonymous feedback).

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: The player receives a hint: "Notice how Maya’s concern was brushed aside and how the silence was taken as agreement. What social dynamic might cause that?"
assessment.follow_up_if_right: The player is praised and receives a tip: "Next time, try suggesting a brief anonymous poll or asking the team to list potential failure modes before finalizing the plan."

game_hooks.npc_personality: Dr. Arlen is charismatic, results‑driven, and subtly intolerant of delays; Maya is diligent, risk‑aware, but prone to self‑doubt under pressure.
game_hooks.npc_dialogue_seed:
Dr. Arlen: "We’ve got a tight window; let’s keep the momentum. Any concerns?"
Maya (after meeting): "I’m uneasy about the off‑target data, but I don’t want to be the obstacle."
Player choice: [1] Press for a deeper review, [2] Suggest a quick side experiment, [3] Accept the plan and move on.
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player challenges the consensus, the lab initiates an optional validation run, uncovering the mutation issue and averting a larger failure. If the player accepts, the story proceeds but later triggers a setback event where the IRB flags the missing risk analysis.

scenario.context: The player is on a cross‑country road trip, driving a caravan of wagons through the kingdom of Valoria. At the crossroads of the Dusty Ridge, they stop at a modest roadside tavern called The Wandering Wheel. While refueling, they meet Mara, a seasoned caravan mechanic who claims to know the best routes.
scenario.text:
Mara leans over the table, pointing at a crumpled flyer stuck to the wall. "I heard the mountain pass to the east is supposed to be closed after the storm last night. But I've always taken that shortcut and never been late, so I know it's fine. The highway will add three hours to our journey, while the pass shaves off two. Trust me, we should cut through the pass." 

The player can:
1) Follow Mara's advice and take the mountain pass without checking any other source.
2) Ask Mara to verify the pass status on the map board or with the town guard before deciding.
3) Insist on staying on the main highway despite Mara's insistence.
scenario.speaker_context: Mara is convinced that the shortcut is always the better choice because it aligns with her belief that speed trumps safety. She dismisses the new information about the pass being potentially closed, rationalizing that her past experiences prove the claim, without seeking external verification.

structure.pattern_description: Mara evaluates the claim about the mountain pass based on whether the conclusion (the pass is usable and faster) matches her pre‑existing belief that shortcuts are always superior. She ignores contradictory evidence (the flyer about a possible closure) and rationalizes the claim to fit her belief, leading to a potentially faulty decision.
structure.formal_form: Agent judges proposition P as true because P aligns with prior belief B, without independently evaluating evidence E that contradicts P.
structure.why_wrong: Mara's confidence in the shortcut is not grounded in current evidence; the storm may have rendered the pass impassable. By letting her belief dictate her judgment, she risks delaying the journey, endangering the caravan, and missing critical supplies. Logical assessment requires weighing the new evidence, not just confirming a favored belief.
structure.counterpoint: When time is extremely limited and reliable evidence is unavailable, relying on trusted personal experience can be a useful heuristic to make quick decisions.

assessment.identification_prompt: Which cognitive bias is Mara displaying when she dismisses the flyer about the mountain pass closure and insists the shortcut is safe because it fits her belief?

rubric.description: No recognition of bias; provides unrelated answer.
Mentions a bias but confuses it with another (e.g., confirmation bias).
Identifies belief bias but gives an incomplete explanation.
Correctly names belief bias and explains that Mara judges the claim based on her prior belief rather than evidence.
Provides a thorough explanation, cites the specific dialogue, and contrasts belief bias with a more appropriate evidence‑based reasoning.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: Mara smiles and says, "I know it sounds risky, but I've always trusted my gut on these shortcuts. Maybe you could check the map for me?" This prompts the player to reconsider the evidence and offers a chance to correct the bias.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Mara nods appreciatively, "Exactly, it's easy to let what we already believe steer us. Let's look at the map together and see if the pass really is open." The player gains a small experience reward for spotting the bias.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Confident, a bit stubborn, values speed and personal experience over paperwork. Friendly but persuasive.
npc_dialogue_seed: I've taken that pass a dozen times; it's never let me down.
The storm? That's just wind—roads stay clear.
Why waste hours on the main road when we can shave time?
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player chooses option 2 (verify), they discover the pass is indeed closed, avoid a dead‑end, and the caravan proceeds safely on the highway. If they choose option 1 (follow blindly), they encounter a landslide, lose supplies, and must backtrack, leading to a lesson about questioning beliefs. Option 3 (stay on highway) avoids the hazard but adds travel time, illustrating the trade‑off between speed and caution.

scenario.text: The alarm blares, red lights flash, and a thin plume of steam curls from the coffee station. Maya clutches her chest and slides onto the floor, coughing. Around her, five employees glance up. Jordan, the team lead, says aloud, "Someone will call the safety officer," and steps back to look at his tablet. A junior analyst, Priya, mutters, "The fire drill will handle it," and returns to her spreadsheet. The office manager, Luis, sighs, "I’m in the middle of a client call, I’ll let someone else handle it," and walks toward the hallway. scenario.speaker_context: Each bystander assumes another person will take responsibility for the emergency, leading to collective paralysis despite the clear need for immediate help.

structure.pattern_description: When an emergency occurs in a group, individuals often defer responsibility to others, assuming someone else will act. This diffusion of responsibility reduces the likelihood that any one person intervenes, even when immediate help is needed.
structure.why_wrong: The presence of many witnesses should increase the chance of assistance, but the bystander effect flips this expectation. Each person’s hesitation compounds, leaving the victim without aid and potentially worsening the outcome.
structure.counterpoint: When a clear, assigned role is given (e.g., "You, Alex, call 911"), the diffusion collapses and action follows. In some cultures, collective norms encourage waiting for official protocols, which can be useful for coordinated responses.

assessment.identification_prompt: After observing the scene, explain why the employees are not stepping in to help Maya and name the cognitive bias at play.

rubric.description: Provides no explanation or mentions an unrelated concept.

Identifies that responsibility is being diffused among the group but does not label the bias.
Correctly names the Bystander Effect and describes diffusion of responsibility, but explanation lacks depth.

Accurately names the Bystander Effect, explains diffusion of responsibility, pluralistic ignorance, and why the alarm and visible crowd paradoxically reduce help, linking it to workplace safety training.

assessment.follow_up_if_wrong: The NPCs are assuming someone else will act, which is a classic sign of the Bystander Effect. In real emergencies, assigning a specific person to take charge can break this pattern. Try to spot how responsibility is being shared in the description.
assessment.follow_up_if_right: Well done! Recognizing the Bystander Effect lets you intervene deliberately—assign a teammate, call emergency services, or apply first aid—overriding the group's inertia.

game_hooks.npc_personality: Jordan is a competent team lead who values order and prefers to let protocols handle crises, making him prone to defer action in ambiguous emergencies.

"The fire drill will sort this out," Priya mutters while scrolling her spreadsheet.
"I’m on a call; let someone else handle it," Luis replies, heading toward the elevator.
game_hooks.resolution_path: If the player steps forward (e.g., shouts for help, calls 911, or administers basic aid), the NPCs will either follow the player's lead, comment on the player's decisiveness, or, if the player hesitates, the scene will progress to a failed outcome, reinforcing the lesson about diffusion of responsibility.
